title: Has the Middle Class Lost Out to the Top 1%? Wealth vs Pay in Charts
description:
In early October 2026, new Federal Reserve figures showed the richest 1% of American households holding a record share of the country's wealth, while the Census Bureau reported that the typical household's income hit a record in 2025.

We separate wealth from pay, show how the slices of America's wealth have shifted since 1989, put a dollar figure on what the middle class lost compared with the top 1%, and check whether pay tells the same story. Our honest take is at the end.
comment: Do you feel better or worse off than your parents were at your age? Tell us your age bracket and why.

scenes.narration: In early October, the Federal Reserve's newest wealth figures made headlines: the richest Americans now own a bigger slice of the country than ever. And a few weeks before that, the Census Bureau said a typical household's income hit a record.

headlines.text: The new K-shaped economy splits the rich from the ultra-rich
Top 1% Hold $60.3 Trillion, Bottom 50% Just $4.3 Trillion: Market Commentator Says 'the Middle Class Is Gone'
Median Household Income in 2025 Surpassed Previous Highs Before and After the COVID-19 Pandemic

scenes.narration: Here are the numbers behind those headlines. In the spring of this year, the top {{ 0.01 | pct }} of American households held {{ latest(top1n) * 1000000 | usd }} of wealth. That is {{ latest(top1) / 100 | pct1 }} of everything households own, the highest share since the Fed's records begin in 1989. Fortune worked out that the top {{ 0.001 | pct }} alone, about {{ latest(households_top01_news) | num }} households, holds {{ latest(top01_news) | pct }}. The whole bottom half of the country, tens of millions of families, held {{ latest(bot50n) * 1000000 | usd }} between them. Meanwhile, the Census Bureau said real median household income rose {{ latest(income_news) | pct1 }} in 2025, to {{ latest(income) | usd }}, a record. One commentator quoted by Benzinga put it bluntly: the middle class is gone. Is that true?

chart.title: A record share at the very top
chart.label: WHAT JUST HAPPENED

scenes.narration: So here is today's question. How much has the middle class lost compared with the top {{ 0.01 | pct }}? To answer it honestly, we need to separate two things that often get mixed up. Pay is what you earn each year. Wealth, or net worth, is what you own minus what you owe: your home, savings, pension pot and shares, minus the mortgage and other debts. The Fed's figures are about wealth. For pay, we will use the Census Bureau's income survey. They tell quite different stories.

chart.title: Has the middle class lost out to the top?
chart.label: WEALTH VS PAY

scenes.narration: Every quarter since 1989, the Federal Reserve splits all household wealth into four groups, ranked by how much they own. The top {{ 0.01 | pct }}. The next {{ 0.09 | pct }}, the comfortably well off. The middle {{ 0.4 | pct }}, everyone from the median household up to the top tenth, which is what we will call the middle class. And the bottom half.

chart.file: File:Marriner S. Eccles Federal Reserve Board Building.jpg
chart.caption: The Federal Reserve, Washington

scenes.narration: Here is how the pie has been sliced. In 1989, the top {{ 0.01 | pct }} held {{ value(top1, "1989-07") / 100 | pct }} of all wealth. Today it is {{ latest(top1) / 100 | pct }}. The middle {{ 0.4 | pct }} went the other way, from {{ value(mid40, "1989-07") / 100 | pct }} to {{ latest(mid40) / 100 | pct }}, close to its lowest on record. The next {{ 0.09 | pct }} barely moved, from {{ value(next9, "1989-07") / 100 | pct }} to {{ latest(next9) / 100 | pct }}. And the bottom half, which never owned much, slipped from {{ value(bot50, "1989-07") / 100 | pct1 }} to {{ latest(bot50) / 100 | pct1 }}. After the housing crash its share fell to just {{ lowest(bot50, "1989", "latest") / 100 | pct1 }} in {{ year_of_lowest(bot50, "1989", "latest") | year }}, because many families' homes were worth less than their mortgages.

chart.title: Who owns America's wealth
chart.subtitle: Share of all household net worth, percent

scenes.narration: Now look at just two lines: the top {{ 0.01 | pct }} and the middle {{ 0.4 | pct }}. In 1989, the middle class owned far more of the country's wealth than the richest households. Early in 2014, the lines crossed for the first time. The middle class drew level or edged ahead again at times, in early 2020 and from 2022 to 2024, but today the top {{ 0.01 | pct }} owns {{ latest(top1) / 100 | pct }} of all wealth, while the far larger middle class owns {{ latest(mid40) / 100 | pct }}.

chart.title: The richest overtook the middle class
chart.subtitle: Share of all household net worth, percent

scenes.narration: Why did this happen? Mostly because of what each group owns. A middle-class family's wealth is mainly its home and a retirement account. The richest hold far more of theirs in company shares and private businesses. Fortune's analysis of the Fed data found that the top {{ 0.001 | pct }} hold {{ latest(stocks01_news) | usd }} in stocks and mutual funds alone, out of nearly {{ latest(wealth01_news) | usd }}. So when the stock market booms, as it has for most of the time since the financial crisis, wealth at the top jumps the most. When house prices rise, the middle class gains, but a home is one asset, often bought with a large mortgage.

chart.query: New York Stock Exchange trading floor
chart.caption: Shares at the top, homes in the middle

scenes.narration: But a smaller slice is not the same as losing money, because the whole pie grew. Here is each group's total wealth in today's dollars, adjusted for inflation. Since 1989, the top {{ 0.01 | pct }}'s wealth rose {{ pct_change(top1w, "1989-07", "latest") | pct }}. The middle {{ 0.4 | pct }}'s rose {{ pct_change(mid40w, "1989-07", "latest") | pct }}. The bottom half's rose {{ pct_change(bot50w, "1989-07", "latest") | pct }}. So the middle class did not lose wealth in dollars. It more than doubled. It just grew far more slowly than wealth at the top.

chart.title: Everyone gained, the top gained most
chart.subtitle: Total net worth in today's dollars, index 1989 = 100

scenes.narration: Here are the same totals as plain dollar amounts. In 1989, in today's money, the top {{ 0.01 | pct }} owned {{ value(top1w, "1989-07") * 1000000 | usd }}, and the middle {{ 0.4 | pct }} owned {{ value(mid40w, "1989-07") * 1000000 | usd }}, much more. Today the top {{ 0.01 | pct }} owns {{ latest(top1w) * 1000000 | usd }}, and the middle class owns {{ latest(mid40w) * 1000000 | usd }}. Remember that the middle group has {{ 40 | num }} times as many households as the top group. So per household, a family in the top {{ 0.01 | pct }} owned about {{ 40 * value(top1w, "1989-07") / value(mid40w, "1989-07") | times }} as much as a middle-class family in 1989. Today it is about {{ 40 * latest(top1w) / latest(mid40w) | times }} as much.

So how much did the middle class lose compared with the top? If the middle {{ 0.4 | pct }} still had its 1989 share of today's wealth, it would own about {{ latest(mid40w) * 1000000 * (value(mid40, "1989-07") / latest(mid40) - 1) | usd }} more than it does. Going by the Fed's count of the very richest households, that group is about {{ latest(households_top01_news) * 1000 * 0.4 | num }} households, so that is roughly {{ latest(mid40w) * 1000000 * (value(mid40, "1989-07") / latest(mid40) - 1) / (latest(households_top01_news) * 1000 * 0.4) / 1000 | num }} thousand dollars per middle-class household. The top {{ 0.01 | pct }}, at its 1989 share, would hold about {{ latest(top1w) * 1000000 * (1 - value(top1, "1989-07") / latest(top1)) | usd }} less than it does. That is more than the middle lost, because the top also gained share from the other groups. This is an accounting what-if, not a refund anyone is owed.

chart.title: What the shift in shares is worth today
chart.subtitle: Today's wealth, re-split at each group's 1989 share

scenes.narration: Now to pay. This is the income of the typical household, the one exactly in the middle, in today's dollars. In 1989 it was {{ value(income, "1989") | usd }}. In 2025 it was {{ latest(income) | usd }}, the highest on record and {{ pct_change(income, "1989", "latest") | pct }} more. It was a bumpy ride. After the financial crisis it fell for years, and only beat its 2007 level in 2016. It dipped again after the pandemic, when prices jumped faster than pay, before reaching this new high. Notice that middle-class wealth grew much faster than middle-class pay, thanks to rising home values and retirement savings.

chart.title: The typical household's income
chart.subtitle: Real median household income, today's dollars

scenes.narration: But the middle is not the top. The Census Bureau also tracks households near the top and bottom of the income ladder. Since 1967, income at the ninetieth percentile, the household that earns more than nine in ten others, rose {{ latest(p90_news) | pct }} after inflation. Income in the middle, and near the bottom, rose about {{ latest(p50_news) | pct }}. In 1967 a household at the ninetieth percentile earned {{ first(ratio_news, "1967", "latest") | times }} as much as one at the tenth. In 2025 it was {{ latest(ratio_news) | times }}. So pay has grown for everyone, but faster at the top.

chart.title: Pay rose fastest near the top
chart.subtitle: Rise in real household income since 1967, Census Bureau

scenes.narration: Now for the model. These are straight trend lines through the yearly averages of the two wealth shares. On trend, the top {{ 0.01 | pct }}'s share has risen about {{ trend_per_year(top1, "1989", "latest") | pts }} a year since 1989, and the middle {{ 0.4 | pct }}'s has fallen about {{ -trend_per_year(mid40, "1989", "latest") | pts }} a year. Those two numbers are close, so as a rough rule, what the middle class lost in share, the very top gained. A trend is not a forecast. Look at the dips. After the dot-com bust, the top share fell from {{ value(top1, "2000-01") / 100 | pct }} early in 2000 to {{ value(top1, "2002-07") / 100 | pct }} in mid-2002. In the financial crisis it fell from {{ value(top1, "2007-07") / 100 | pct }} to {{ value(top1, "2009-01") / 100 | pct }}. So a long stock market slump can pull the top share down fast. But each time, the trend came back.

chart.title: A slow, steady shift
chart.subtitle: Share of household net worth, percent, yearly averages with fitted trend

scenes.narration: So, has the middle class lost out to the top {{ 0.01 | pct }}? In share, yes, clearly. The middle {{ 0.4 | pct }} owns a much smaller slice of the country's wealth than in 1989, and the top {{ 0.01 | pct }} now owns more than the whole middle class. In dollars, no. Middle-class wealth more than doubled after inflation, and median household income is at a record. The middle class is not gone. It is a smaller slice of a much bigger pie, and the gap between it and the very top has widened over these decades.

chart.title: A smaller slice of a bigger pie
chart.label: THE ANSWER

scenes.narration: Here is my take, and it is an opinion. For an ordinary household, the share matters less day to day than whether its own income and savings grow, and on that score the last decade has been better than the one before. But shares still matter, because wealth brings security, the ability to help children and a louder voice in public life, and that is now concentrated further than at any time in these records. Much of the gap comes from owning shares versus not owning them. What would change my mind? A long fall in share prices, or several years of faster pay growth in the middle, would show the trend reversing.

method: Wealth shares and totals come from the Federal Reserve's Distributional Financial Accounts; totals are restated in today's dollars with the consumer price index. The what-if re-splits today's total wealth at each group's 1989 share; households per group are estimated from the Fed's count of the top 0.1% as reported by Fortune. The model fits a straight line through the yearly average shares.
